[[File:Classical gel vs. Olympic gel.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Comparison of the network structures of a classical polymer gel and an Olympic gel.<ref name="x274">{{cite journal | last1=Speed | first1=Sarah K. | last2=Peng | first2=Yu-Hsuan | last3=Atabay | first3=Azra | last4=Gupta | first4=Krishna | last5=Müller | first5=Toni | last6=Fischer | first6=Carolin | last7=Hermes | first7=Ilka M. | last8=Sommer | first8=Jens-Uwe | last9=Lang | first9=Michael | last10=Krieg | first10=Elisha | title=Assembling a True "Olympic Gel" from over 16 000 Combinatorial DNA Rings | journal=Advanced Materials | volume=38 | date=2026 | article-number=e20549 | doi=10.1002/adma.202520549 | pmid=41789447 | doi-access=free }}</ref>]]An '''Olympic gel''' is a type of [[material]] made of [[polymer]] molecules that are connected like the rings in the [[Olympic symbol]]. Each pair of linked molecules forms a [[catenane]], and Olympic gels may be considered a type of [[mechanically interlocked molecular architecture]]. The name and concept originate with the work of [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]],<ref name="o884">{{cite journal | last1=Raphaël | first1=E. | last2=Gay | first2=C. | last3=de Gennes | first3=P. G. | title=Progressive construction of an "Olympic" gel | journal=Journal of Statistical Physics | volume=89 | issue=1–2 | date=1997 | issn=0022-4715 | doi=10.1007/BF02770756 | pages=111–118 | bibcode=1997JSP....89..111R | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02770756 | access-date=2025-08-24| url-access=subscription }}</ref> and an illustration of an Olympic gel appears on the cover of certain editions of his book ''Scaling Concepts in Polymer Physics''. They are initially of interest to the [[materials physics]] community due to their predicted nonlinear [[Elasticity (physics)|elasticity]],<ref name="l702">{{cite journal | last1=Vilgis | first1=Thomas A. | last2=Otto | first2=Matthias | title=Elasticity of entangled polymer loops: Olympic gels | journal=Physical Review E | volume=56 | issue=2 | date=1997-08-01 | issn=1063-651X | doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.56.R1314 | doi-access=free | pages=R1314–R1317 | arxiv=cond-mat/9705285 | bibcode=1997PhRvE..56.1314V }}</ref> stretching differently than a [[Hookean]] material with different behavior at low and high forces.

The existence of [[enzymes]] that can modify the [[topology]] of [[DNA]] allows the construction of Olympic gels from DNA in various ways. One method uses [[Topoisomerase II]] to form links between circular molecules such as [[plasmids]], which in high enough density allows the formation of an Olympic gel.<ref name="v589">{{cite journal | last1=Krajina | first1=Brad A. | last2=Zhu | first2=Audrey | last3=Heilshorn | first3=Sarah C. | last4=Spakowitz | first4=Andrew J. | title=Active DNA Olympic Hydrogels Driven by Topoisomerase Activity | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=121 | issue=14 | date=2018-10-01 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.148001 | doi-access=free | article-number=148001 | pmid=30339454 | bibcode=2018PhRvL.121n8001K }}</ref> Another method uses [[Watson-Crick base pairing]] with complimentary sequences on opposite ends of linear DNA molecules. If there are enough unique sequences of DNA in a sample, molecules are more likely to form loops than [[concatemers]], and after [[Ligation (molecular biology)|ligation]] an Olympic gel can be formed.<ref name="x274">{{cite journal | last1=Speed | first1=Sarah K. | last2=Peng | first2=Yu-Hsuan | last3=Atabay | first3=Azra | last4=Gupta | first4=Krishna | last5=Müller | first5=Toni | last6=Fischer | first6=Carolin | last7=Hermes | first7=Ilka M. | last8=Sommer | first8=Jens-Uwe | last9=Lang | first9=Michael | last10=Krieg | first10=Elisha | title=Assembling a True "Olympic Gel" from over 16 000 Combinatorial DNA Rings | journal=Advanced Materials | volume=38 | date=2026 | article-number=e20549 | doi=10.1002/adma.202520549 | pmid=41789447 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Naturally occurring Olympic gels are found in [[kinetoplast]] DNA in the [[mitochondria]] of [[Trypanosoma|trypanosome]] parasites. Kinetoplasts consist of thousands of linked DNA circular DNA molecules, in which smaller molecules are transcribed into [[RNA]] molecules that can edit the RNA transcribed from [[mitochondrial DNA]].

There have been reports of synthetic Olympic gels created from [[hydroxyethyl lipoate]].<ref name="a679">{{cite journal | last1=Xiong | first1=Xinhong | last2=Xue | first2=Mingju | last3=Xue | first3=Lulu | last4=Zhang | first4=Luzhi | last5=Zhang | first5=Zhongyan | last6=Chen | first6=Jian | last7=Zhang | first7=Guojie | last8=Liu | first8=Hong | last9=Cui | first9=Jiaxi | title=Evaporation-Assisted Synthesis of Olympic Gels | journal=Angewandte Chemie | publisher=Wiley | volume=137 | issue=22 | date=2025-02-10 | issn=0044-8249 | doi=10.1002/ange.202425034 | doi-access=free | article-number=e202425034 | bibcode=2025AngCh.137E5034X }}</ref>
